{{Short description|American experimental physicist}}
{{Infobox scientist|birth_date=17 February 1927|death_date=10 May 1986|death_place=[[Los Angeles]], California, US|field=experimental physics|education ={{hlist|[[University of Colorado]]|[[University of Pittsburgh]]}}|doctoral_advisor=[[David Halliday (physicist)|David Halliday]]}}

'''John Charles Wheatley''' (17 February 1927, Tucson – 10 May 1986, [[Los Angeles]]) was an American experimental physicist who worked on quantum fluids at low and very low temperatures.<ref name=PhysToday>{{cite journal|author=Vilches, Oscar|title=John C. Wheatley|journal=Physics Today|date=September 1986|volume=39|issue=9|pages=73–74|url=http://www.physicstoday.org/resource/1/phtoad/v39/i9/p73_s2?bypassSSO=1|doi=10.1063/1.2815154|bibcode=1986PhT....39i..73V}}{{Dead link|date=February 2020 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Pushing the Limits: John Wheatley (1927–1986)|journal=[[Los Alamos Science]]|date=Fall 1986|pages=35–47|url=http://www.fas.org/sgp/othergov/doe/lanl/pubs/00326879.pdf}}</ref>

==Biography==
Wheatley received his B.S. in electrical engineering in 1947 from the [[University of Colorado]] in Boulder and his Ph.D. in physics under [[David Halliday (physicist)|David Halliday]] in 1952 from the [[University of Pittsburgh]]. From 1952 to 1966 he was an instructor and then a professor at the [[University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign]]. In 1966 he became a full professor in the physics department of the [[University of California, San Diego]]. From 1981 to 1985 he did research at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]] as a permanent staff member of the Laboratory. From 1985 he was a professor at the [[University of California, Los Angeles|UCLA]].<ref name=AIP>{{Cite web |url=http://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?wheatleyj |title=Biography from AIP |access-date=2013-09-09 |archive-date=2016-03-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307143744/https://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?wheatleyj |url-status=dead }}</ref> He died of a heart attack while riding a bicycle.<ref name=LATimes>{{cite news|title=John Wheatley, 59, Physics Scholar|newspaper=LA Times|date=15 March 1986|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1986-03-15-fi-21095-story.html}}</ref>

His fame stems from his research on liquid [[helium-3]], a Fermi liquid. He collaborated with theorists such as [[John Bardeen]], [[Gordon Baym]], and Christopher Pethick. In the academic years 1954/55 and 1980/81 he was a [[Guggenheim Fellow]]<ref>{{cite web|title=John C. Wheatley|website=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation|url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/john-c-wheatley/}}</ref> at the [[University of Leiden]]. He was elected a Fellow of the American Physical Society in 1961.<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1961&unit_id=&institution=University+of+Illinois}}</ref> He was a [[Sloan Fellow]]. In 1965/66 he was a guest scientist at the Center for Advanced Study of the University of Illinois in Urbana-Champaign. He was also a guest scientist for 18 months in 1962/63 at [[Bariloche Atomic Centre]] in Argentina, where he helped to establish a low temperature laboratory. At the time of his death he had been nominated for UCLA's first Presidential Chair in Physics. In 1975 Wheatley won the [[Fritz London Memorial Prize]] and in 1966 the [[Simon Memorial Prize]]. He was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1975 and he was also a member of the Finnish Academy of Sciences.<ref name="PhysToday"/> In 1991 the [[John Wheatley Award]] was established in his honor.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://research.fit.edu/fip/wheatley_award1.htm |title=Wheatley Award, the Forum on International Physics |access-date=2013-09-09 |archive-date=2012-02-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120208065347/http://research.fit.edu/fip/wheatley_award1.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref>

He had a wife and two sons.<ref name="LATimes"/>

==SHE Corporation==
In 1970 Wheatley founded the SHE (for Superconducting Helium Electronics) Corporation in San Diego with [[Olli Lounasmaa]] and other colleagues. SHE was the first worldwide corporation specializing in superconducting electronics.<ref name=":0">{{cite book |last1=Johnson |first1=R. T. |title=Magnetic Source Imaging of the Human Brain |last2=Hirschkoff |first2=E. C. |last3=Buchanan |first3=D. S. |publisher=Psychology Press |year=2013 |isbn=978-1135625672 |editor=Lu |editor-first=Zhong-Lin |chapter=Full-Sensitivity Biomagnetometers: Sam Williamson's Vision Brought to Life |doi=10.4324/9781410609175-8 |editor2=Kaufman |editor-first2=Lloyd |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mH0lIHdChVgC&pg=PT225}}</ref> The name of the corporation was changed to Biomagnetic Technologies, Inc. (BTi) in 1985, and in December 1999, BTi merged with the Finnish company Neuromag Oy to form the new corporation 4-D Neuroimaging.<ref name=":0" /> The Neuromag part of the company was sold to Elekta AB of Sweden in 2003; 4-D Neuroimaging filed for bankruptcy in 2009.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://guide.ieeecsc.org/ |title=The 4-D Company Closed its Doors – European Superconductivity News Forum |access-date=2024-07-31 |archive-date=2024-07-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240729073247/http://guide.ieeecsc.org/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>[http://www.wtec.org/loyola/scel96/06_02.htm Ch6: History of SQUID Technology in the United States and Japan]</ref>
